analysis.one_liner: Taxes half of oil producers' windfall profits above $40 a barrel and returns the money as home-heating aid and consumer rebates.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 11 cosponsors in November 2005, sent to three House committees, and never received a hearing, a vote, or a floor debate before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have imposed a 50% excise tax on crude oil producers' profits above $40 a barrel (adjusted for inflation), with the tax expiring after three years. Revenue would have gone into a new Consumer Energy Assistance Trust Fund to pay for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance program, which helps poor households pay heating bills, and the rest would have been rebated to taxpayers. The bill excluded newly discovered oil and credited companies for investments in refineries, drilling, and renewable fuel facilities.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households that receive LIHEAP home-energy assistance, and taxpayers generally through the energy consumer rebate. Oil producers who invested in new refineries, drilling, or renewable fuels would have reduced their tax by those qualified investments.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 50% excise tax on crude oil producers' net windfall profit, defined as the sales price of a barrel of crude oil above an inflation-adjusted base price of $40 per barrel, with the tax ending three years after enactment [S2].

Creates a Consumer Energy Assistance Trust Fund in the Treasury, deposits all windfall tax revenue into it, and makes the money available to fund the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Act, the federal program that helps poor households pay heating and cooling bills [S2].

Grants every eligible taxpayer an income tax rebate sized by the Treasury Secretary based on the number of taxpayers and available windfall tax revenue, with payments deemed made February 1 and remitted within 30 days [S3].

Reduces producers' tax by their qualified investments, including intangible drilling costs, qualified refinery property, renewable electricity facilities, and alcohol, biodiesel, and agri-biodiesel fuel production facilities [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Crude oil producers, who would pay the 50% excise tax on profits above the $40-per-barrel base price. In 2005, with oil prices well above that level after hurricanes disrupted supply, the tax would have clawed back a large share of producers' windfall gains.

drawbacks.text: Economists have long argued that windfall profits taxes discourage oil production and can raise consumer prices; this bill tried to blunt that by excluding newly discovered oil from the tax and crediting producers for drilling, refinery, and renewable fuel investments, but oil from already-proven fields would still face the tax, which could reduce supply [S3].

The rebate amount was left entirely to the Treasury Secretary, based on whatever revenue the tax collected after the LIHEAP appropriation, so households could not know in advance how much, if any, rebate they would receive [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design tried to have it both ways: it taxed windfall profits but carved out new drilling and credited refinery and renewable investments, which softens the main economic objection that such a tax deters production. The consumer benefits were real but partly uncertain — LIHEAP funding would depend on tax collections, and the rebate was discretionary. On balance, it was a targeted transfer from oil producers' 2005-2008 price windfall to low-income energy consumers and taxpayers, with modest supply-side risk thanks to the exemptions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees and then to subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing; Markey tried to force it to the floor with a discharge petition, but that never succeeded and the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey introduced the bill on November 9, 2005, joined by Reps. Emanuel, Sanders, Nadler, and Hinchey; it was referred to the Committees on Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Education and the Workforce [S1].
The bill gained 11 cosponsors (10 Democrats and 1 Independent) but no further action from any of the three committees [S4].

In April 2006, Markey filed a motion to discharge the committee — a procedure to pull a bill out of committee and onto the floor over the committee's objection, which requires a majority of House members to sign a petition [S5].
No discharge petition signatures, hearing, markup, or floor vote followed, and the bill expired at the end of the 109th Congress in January 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil producers kept their windfall profits untaxed, and Congress never redirected any of them to home-heating assistance or consumer rebates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil producers, whose windfall profits stayed untaxed

for.name: Rep. Edward J. Markey
for.role: U.S. Representative (MA-7); bill sponsor; filed the discharge petition
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, recruited cosponsors, and filed a discharge petition in an attempt to bring it to the House floor without committee action.

for.name: Reps. Emanuel, Sanders, Nadler, and Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Joined Markey as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral; never held a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the House calendar and committee chairmanships in the 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: No committee chaired by the majority ever scheduled the bill, and the discharge petition never gathered the signatures needed to force a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 11 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Rep. Sanders; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced in the Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: Producers would have paid a 50% excise tax on crude oil sold above $40 a barrel, but the bill excluded newly discovered oil and credited producers for drilling, refinery, and renewable fuel investments, softening the hit. The bill died, so producers kept their 2005-2008 price windfall untaxed.
All windfall tax revenue would have flowed to the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance program, directly increasing help for poor households' heating bills. It never received the money.

Qualified refinery property and alcohol, biodiesel, and agri-biodiesel facilities counted as qualified investment, reducing a producer's windfall tax bill — an incentive built into the tax rather than a direct benefit, and it never took effect.
